# About this class

Introduction to R and RStudio, basic calculations, data types, vectors, matrices, lists, factors and data frames.

These notes are organized as a standalone R Markdown lesson. Run the code chunks in order and use **Knit** in RStudio to generate the report.

# 1. Introduction to R and RStudio

R is a programming language and environment used for statistical computing, data analysis and visualization. RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) that makes working with R easier.

An R Markdown (`.Rmd`) document combines text, R code and the output generated by that code. When you **Knit** the document, R executes the code chunks and produces a report.

## 1.1 Basic calculations

```{r basic-calculations}
2 + 3
10 / 2
5^2
sqrt(81)
log(10)
```

Assign values to objects using `<-`.

```{r assignment}
x <- 10
y <- 5
total <- x + y
total
```

## 1.2 Important definitions in data science

- **Statistics:** collecting, organizing, analyzing and interpreting data.
- **Modelling:** representing relationships or processes using mathematical or statistical models.
- **Computation:** using computers to process data and perform calculations.
- **Calculus:** mathematical study of change and accumulation.

# 2. R data structures and data types

## 2.1 Common data types

```{r data-types}
numeric_values <- c(0.5, 0.6, 2.8)
integer_values <- 9:15
logical_values <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
character_values <- c("A", "B", "C")
complex_values <- c(1 + 0i, 2 + 4i)

class(numeric_values)
class(integer_values)
class(logical_values)
class(character_values)
class(complex_values)
```

## 2.2 Vectors

A vector stores values of the same basic type.

```{r vectors}
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
summary(age)
mean(age)
length(age)
age[2]
```

## 2.3 Matrices

A matrix is a two-dimensional structure in which all elements have the same data type.

```{r matrices}
x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2)

x
y
x %*% y
```

## 2.4 Lists

A list can contain elements of different data types.

```{r lists}
my_list <- list(
  score = 85,
  student = "Alex",
  passed = TRUE,
  result = 1 + 4i
)

my_list
my_list$student
```

## 2.5 Factors

Factors represent categorical variables. They are useful for nominal and ordinal data.

```{r factors}
response <- factor(c("Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "No"))
response
levels(response)

education <- factor(
  c("Primary", "University", "Secondary", "University"),
  levels = c("Primary", "Secondary", "University"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
education
```

## 2.6 Data frames

A data frame stores data in rows and columns. Different columns can have different data types.

```{r data-frame}
studentID <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
gender <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
it_score <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)

scoredata <- data.frame(studentID, gender, math_score, it_score)
scoredata
str(scoredata)
summary(scoredata)
```

## 2.7 Missing values and data coercion

`NA` represents a missing value. Use `is.na()` to identify missing observations and `complete.cases()` to identify rows with no missing values in selected variables.

```{r missing-values}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)
is.na(x)
x[!is.na(x)]

a <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
b <- c("A", "B", NA, "D")
complete.cases(a, b)
```

R may coerce values to a common type when different types are combined in one vector.

```{r coercion}
mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")
mixed
class(mixed)

sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))
```
